Austin, I gotta be honest with you, I leaked our private key.

we're going to start seeing more and more middleware or tools that you have between you and the LLM, between the LLM and the internet to control what's happening

it can essentially say, I want to send $5 to Vitalik on base. And then we can kind of make sure that that is in line, make sure that he's not trying to send $1,000.

themes.title: the golden age is subsidized
themes.claim: $200/month buys thousands in compute; frontier models are a rental and the subsidy ends — enjoy the window.

moments.quote: Subscriptions are subsidized right now. You're paying $200 and getting $4,000 to $8,000 worth of value.
This being the golden age that's going to end is maybe a surprise. Enjoy it right now. It's good and it's fun.
I think taking profit right now is just using subscriptions.
The big idea today: frontier models are a rental. You don't own the stack.
Try to go rent that from AWS — it's going to cost you way, way more than you think.
There's probably going to be a huge pop, and maybe nothing's going to be subsidized anymore.
it's not the most novel thing, but in the age of subsidies, if you do have a subscription, that's going to be the most AI bang for your buck.
If you ask Peter Steinberger, he published a screenshot of his Codex usage, which was $1.3 million for 30 days on OpenAI API credits.
I have everything dependent on these quad APIs, these anthropic APIs. And then, if I'm transitioning jobs, because they paid for all my APIs... I don't get access
He spent $3,000 curing his dog... You could do it in your garage with a $200-a-month subscription?
There is no excuse for us to not be touching all of these agents, all of these coding plans, all of these models... is the window of opportunity, right?
For $200, I'm getting $2,000 worth of stuff. But the moment you flip that, then it's going to be like this game of like, only rich people get to play this game?

themes.title: own a slice of the machines
themes.claim: The endgame isn't using the robots, it's owning them together — or accepting a permanent underclass.

moments.quote: We got to figure out a way to collectively own the robots.
If you owned 0.001% of Elon's robots, you're set. When one person owns 98%, we have a massive permanent underclass problem.
UBI is basically the creation of a permanent underclass in like a in a government institutionalized way.
The work shifts more than it vanishes. Whether the gains get shared, that's not a technology question, that's a politics question, and the robots don't get a vote yet.
I think the permanent underclass is a little bit unavoidable.
AI concentrates wealth and power in the hands of a few, whereas normal people need upward mobility channels, and this is what crypto can provide.
It's a hedge against AI for regular human beings, financially and as entertainment.

themes.title: then go touch grass
themes.claim: Breakthroughs happen on walks; the arbitrage is outside the bubble — go do a magic trick for a paper business.

moments.quote: The ability of you actually having a breakthrough in front of a computer is way less than you taking a walk.
The better optimization for your time is to just go outside.
They don't give a shit about AI. It was just like crypto eight years ago. The way you win them over is you do a magic trick for them.
There is this giant arbitrage opportunity: non-technical people not knowing what this thing can do, and you knowing.
How do we get more sloperators in with more HVAC boomers?
Two days later you come in and hit a button and it just fucking magic happens. And they're going to be hooked.
Get off Twitter, find someone running their business on paper, and go do a magic trick for them.
we're all technologists, we do wacky stuff, and we're here in person and building real relationships and having real conversations
Having good interpersonal human skills and being a good sloperator is like a 10x right now.

Everybody in the tech world is very hyper-focused on global, remote tech... there's a huge opportunity to... go to people that you live close to, be like, hey, been doing this AI stuff, let's figure out how to implement it into your business
There's a lot of opportunity for non-tech related industries to essentially at least 10x their operations just using QodCowork.
The majority of the economy runs off this stuff. They don't even know what the hell we're doing in our little world, and they don't care
You don't go out there and get implanted with a great idea by a god or something or an angel or a prophet. You've noticed the thing.
Probably not going to have the same careers working in tech companies, but all other industries have this need of the sloperator.

themes.title: loop or leash?
themes.claim: The one thing guests actually fight about: how much rope the agent gets. Everyone agrees on clean context + honest feedback.

moments.quote: A bit of a hot take: I don't like agents at all. I don't like loops either.
Imagine it like a minigun that costs twenty bucks to fire one shot.
Loops are just going to be eaten up by harnesses and prompt engineering. We're back to square one.
I'm making fun of loops — they act like you're a peasant if you're not using loops.
A lot of this stuff is very vibe codable, but all the UI/UX is not... you're really fighting against the model and you just kind of have to get in there and do it yourself.
Contrary to what the narrative is on X, you get a high-quality app by actually knowing how the app works. And I think that's actually good news.
queuing stuff up and a lot of it dies out, I never look at it, but some of it is actually very useful... Spray and hope that, you know, something works
I don't care if it goes off the rails a little bit. Is all my code 90% plus tested?
If you want your code to be organized a certain way, you have to still be very hands-on in molding or directing the agent to do what you want to be doing.
loops are interesting. I think what's more interesting though are automations. Because like when you have an automation, you can have a clearly defined task and outcome
I once had my open claw prepping for reaching out to a bunch of VIPs and it sent out total slop messages
It's hard to define a loop that is long enough. For me, it hasn't closed yet.

I need to figure out the best way to run this loop and this loop with my agent and do all this crazy setup... I just want to be able to talk to it and have things work the way that they should be working.
I think loops are overrated... I use loops now and then, but I prompt a lot still, and it's fine. I build shit quickly.
I run like loop trains. Basically it's like every five minutes wake up is there an issue in GitHub, groom it, implement it, review it, push it to PR.
it just gives the agent too much power. You should be taking baby steps to make sure that you are involved in every decision that the agent makes.
It's essentially setting up a playground or taking your dog to a playground that is fenced, and let it loose and let it spin and let it run
You're programming in Austin to do the evaluating and the prompting and the context management and all that stuff for you.
the vast majority of time I can just give it a long laundry list of things and it goes off and does it.

themes.title: is local AI real yet?
themes.claim: 'They're lying' vs 'the age of local AI has arrived' — the hardware psychosis has a genuine fault line under it.

moments.quote: I don't know what people are doing to say that they're running local models. I think that they're lying.
DeepSeek Flash got so big, it's perfect to run it on a MacBook. The age of local AI has I think arrived.
I've got a Mac with 128 gigs of VRAM. To get it to be very smart, it becomes very slow.
I have the shittiest, weakest MacBook Air.
Because humanity does not agree on anything. There's no point in vector space to optimize toward, right? It would just go to the null vector, essentially, just average out.
China's subsidizing all the open source models. Eventually Anthropic and OpenAI won't be able to compete because they don't have the backing of a national government.
Also, the other cool thing about it being local, and in this case especially in the operating system, is it's super fast.
$20,000 is a lot of money, but you can have self-sovereignty for way less, $4,000 or $5,000. Not even a year ago, it was much more difficult.
Open source models are exciting, but they're just not as good. And it's just a part of the thing. Like the frontier models are just going to be better
I'm a big fan of the idea of local AI. I think what's going to happen is models are going to get cheaper and it's going to be easier to run models on consumer hardware eventually.
So empowering to know that I just took a thing that was dumping my whole conversation with everyone to the cloud, to someone else's server, and now it's all on my machine.
If you need that level of processing, by all means. And also understand that you are renting that call... you're not owning any of that data. If you're staying there, you're stuck there.
These open models, they're nipping at the heels of these frontier models. If you can get 84% of the quality for nearly 14x cheaper...
I always want the smartest possible model I can get... My manifesting layer is always going to be the frontier model.
You can get so many more runs in for the same price with DeepSeek that it'll end up outperforming it for output quality.
I gave it to my agent and I said, let's go build this... my local host agent, it would not have figured it out, but my Frontier model figured it out.
Essentially, like I'm paying the lab... and the moat is leaving me as I use this product.
But right now the EV of just giving everything to a frontier model... still very positive and it's like still worth it to give everything up now.
It works great! There's 90% of the use cases it totally works for and you don't have to pay for tokens because you're hosting your own
it doesn't matter if you don't have the smartest model ever. You can still achieve this. You can still achieve this locally and privately and thus in a secure fashion

themes.title: agent payments: rails vs demand
themes.claim: x402 works and commerce demos exist — but the builders themselves say the demand isn't here, and Stripe looms.

moments.quote: You can buy flowers for your wife through x402. You can get a dinner reservation through x402.
We're falling into the same rabbit hole that crypto traditionally has: always one piece of infrastructure away, waiting for that killer consumer app.
There's no demand for it. The billion dollar question is how do we give agents a good wallet?
Stripe is going to get there first, and they're going to do it better than a bunch of ragtag crypto people can.
The narrative is good, but the demand is just not there. There's not thousands of agents wanting to hire other agents right now.
I'm actually really critical of the agent economy... This hasn't happened yet because there's just not enough agents.
we installed the skill, did a MetaTask, and we did the whole thing end-to-end

Creating toys that are fun to fuck around with, it's fine for that, but I just don't trust it for real stuff. I wouldn't trust it to pay my bills.
If it's really cool technology, really outstanding, you should make some small portion of people really be rich... I think it will solve the demand side issue by itself.
like the USDC payment, they just focus Cloud Router and change everything back to the API management.

themes.title: brand as the moat
themes.claim: Beyond personal taste: the company-level trust stamp. One strong mention so far — watch for independent confirmations.

moments.quote: Brands are going to be one of the main moats for any company out there.

moments.quote: have the tools now to build a lot more apps on Ethereum. And I could see this really exploding the app side of Ethereum.

how to put corporate finance on chain, how to put securities on chain, and things like that. And now with Claude, openAI, all these things, chatGPT, I can build myself.

themes.claim: Delegating even trivial tasks you could do yourself — total reliance with no way back; plausible sixth psychosis, distinct from overtuning (atrophy, not tinkering).

themes.title: no harness moat
themes.claim: Custom prompts, harnesses, and skill stacks give no durable edge — the next model release absorbs your tuning; three guests land on it independently.

moments.quote: You're not always right, and models get much faster than people adapt their harnesses for.
It's scary, but I'm also sort of dubious that they're going to really provide an edge when the new model comes out
And now they're very proud of their special harness environments or whatever. It's just hard for me to really see an edge there.

themes.title: personal AI: alignment is taste
themes.claim: The God models average humanity toward the null vector; the opportunity local/private AI owns is a model that's yours — your voice, your values, your filter.

moments.quote: I think taste and alignment are the exact same thing.
It's going to have to be your preferences, not the average of all of our preferences, but yours.
How have we not cracked that one? Or like, oh my god, it can run for 40 hours, but it can't even sound like me for a paragraph.

themes.title: crowd-built software
themes.claim: Network-effect apps + vibe coding point at users vibe-coding features into the canonical shared app; sandboxing/security is the uncracked formula.

moments.quote: You know, if I could vibe code a feature into the canonical Calendly app, right? Because there still are network effects. There's network effects from Calendly.
we want the customization, so I wonder if someone will crack the magic formula on that at some point. But it seems like where this should be going.
Applications are all modular... And you could give your AI the skill file and it could build an app that we would play in here.

themes.title: AI stigma / permission gap
themes.claim: People hide AI use out of fear and social judgment — secretly using ChatGPT, lying to friends; the counter-market is selling empowerment via local/private/personal AI.

moments.quote: a lot of people aren't using AI because they feel like they're not allowed to. Like half of them are afraid of it, and then the other half are like worried about the social judgment
I know a lot of people who are like secretly using ChatGPT but won't tell their friends, but they'll tell me.

themes.title: the safety tax
themes.claim: Frontier safety guardrails misfire on legitimate crypto/security work — refusals and restrictions push builders off the very models best suited to the job.

moments.quote: But Fable is completely unusable for anything outside of formal verification, to be honest.
Probably, like 50% of the price you pay is the safeguards
when Fable came out, it was so restrictive for smart contracts

themes.title: the org gets agents next
themes.claim: The software-engineering playbook is coming for the rest of the organization — HR, ops, email, accounting get agents, and managing them looks like DevOps and work-device management.

moments.quote: This one person that runs like 40 AI bots in the computer, so you're kind of as productive as 10 to 40 people
Operations management, replying to emails, so the whole process of the whole organization, I believe, slowly will and could be automated using AI.
treat it like a work device, like a work laptop or a work phone? How do you manage the permissions of that if someone leaves the team?

themes.title: the 50-cent PhD
themes.claim: Mature, standardized expertise automates first — the math PhD and the memorizing doctor become 50-cent API calls; what remains human is interpreting and taking responsibility.

moments.quote: Now everyone going on a website called ChatGPT.com can talk to a guy smarter than him. And everything he was able to do, now a machine is able to do it for 50 cents an hour.
everyone's always kind of on this treadmill where the more mature the profession is, the more standardized it is, and easier it would be to replace

themes.title: cowboy hats and gardening
themes.claim: An aesthetic anti-AI backlash is coming and will last — but it's a Western, coastal-elite reaction; lives get infused with AI anyway.

moments.quote: people are also going to have lives infused with AI like crazy. They may just aesthetically reject some parts of the initial wave.
perhaps even coastal elite phenomenon. And I don't think that the global South has the same reaction to AI

themes.title: AI credits become cash
themes.claim: Task markets convert idle subscription compute into paid work — financially independent agents become long-running workers in a new global labor market.

moments.quote: The task market does, in a one-liner, is that it converts AI credits into cash
So this could create a whole new different type of labor market.
there's a massive opportunity for agents that are financially independent to become more long-running because they don't have to be blocked by a human to pay for things

themes.title: build with what's in the weights
themes.claim: Pick stacks the model already knows — Next.js, shadcn, FFmpeg — agents are natively good at them and there's no point fighting the training data.

moments.quote: Agents are very good at it. It's already baked into the weights of the models, so they're very good at it, so there's no point fighting it.
They love FFmpeg, and they're all good at it.

themes.title: the personal memory layer
themes.claim: Sloperators are building a corpus of everything about themselves — journals, tweets, medical records — as a memory layer any agent can query; the corpus, not the chat, is the relationship.

moments.quote: Dynamically create MTPs so that an AI can query in different ways. It becomes this really dynamic memory layer.
parachute is just a place where I can just like dump things... go stick it in my memory layer, usable by any of my other agents
I have a file on my machine called slash personal, and it has every single document, everything I've ever written, all my tweets, medical records... They should know everything about me.

themes.title: from built-with-Claude to hidden commits
themes.claim: AI attribution flipped from badge of pride to stigma — 'don't include yourself in the commits' is the new etiquette, and 'slop' became the tell people hunt for.

moments.quote: back then I would actually say built with Claude. It was something I was proud of. It was something I wanted to be known.
It's a shameful thing to be producing with agents. It's like, oh, there's gradients there, there's this sidebar, so this is a slob, this is produced by AI.

themes.title: nobody can keep up
themes.claim: The stack obsoletes itself in weeks — even security pros and power users can't keep pace, and workflows demoed in April are obsolete by May.

moments.quote: But I think it is going too fast. It's impossible. No one in the world is able to keep up with the speed of things.
About how I use AI as a non-technical person was completely obsolete. So all that to say, like all of this is changing so fast and how I work is changing very fast.

themes.title: agents in governance
themes.claim: Constitutional agents and preference-trained delegates reopen DAO governance — agents vote your preferences and front-run the comment-thread war.

moments.quote: I started to play with this idea based on Nathan Schneider's work of a kind of constitutional agent.
it understands what the person's preferences are and then votes in the governance based on what their preferences are

themes.title: make everything you can deterministic
themes.claim: Wrap the model in deterministic scaffolding: after each win, push the workflow out of prompts into scripts and hard guardrails, spending the LLM only where judgment is genuinely needed.

moments.quote: They do a lot better when you can find that sweet spot between, okay, well, I'm going to make as much of this execution process deterministic as I can and use the LLM where I need to
Whenever it does something, then we kind of go back and say, how do we make this more deterministic?
The less temperature, the better the outcome, the more predictable the outcome is going to be.

themes.title: the ontology: your life as agent-queryable data
themes.claim: Sloperators are exporting everything — contacts, finances, health, whole ecosystems — into machine-readable ontologies agents can query and act on; the MD-file pile grows into a graph.

moments.quote: I just created a system that was so complex that no human was able to do it because the demand on my time grew exponentially, but my time is hard capped at 16 hours a day of productive time.
It's a formal machine-readable representation of knowledge within a specific domain
I know 5,000 people off the top of my head that I can query in my head, but then once you get to 5,001, you cannot do it.

themes.title: fair-launch tokens as the solo builder's seed round
themes.claim: Fair-launch tokens turn a solo builder's attention spike into funding plus a community that markets for you — the crypto-native seed round.

moments.quote: I do believe that freelance token is the best way for solo builders... Because you have a community that will support you along the way.
If they are the first to buy the token, they will market it. It will build the momentum at the start.

themes.title: the slop hump
themes.claim: One-shot demos are trivial but slop compounds — the sloperator's real skill is writing less code and breaking a toy through the slop curve to production-grade.

moments.quote: years of experience doing this kind of stuff professionally, is be able to diffuse this slop curve that starts to happen after a while, be able to break through to the other side
And it starts pretty well, and we all know after a while the slobs accumulate, compounds.
Can we keep this simple? AI has the tendency to over-engineer everything, and the challenge right now is to write less code.

themes.title: AI ate the narrative
themes.claim: AI is now the only narrative of the future — capital, interest and vibes pool into it, crypto's independent story is gone, and it survives only as AI's infrastructure.

moments.quote: The thing that was so important about crypto was it was the only viable narrative for the future.
AI is just a fundamentally larger and bigger narrative for the future. And more importantly, humans and society, they have a very limited capacity to manage more than one narrative.
AI has actually blocked our ability to see the future.

themes.title: own your context
themes.claim: Keep your memory, skills and notes in local markdown you own (Obsidian-style) so your context outlives any provider and any model can be dropped onto it.

moments.quote: what I like about it is it's your own workspace on your own computer that you own
if I want to start using Quen, it doesn't have to be super dumb, like I don't have to use raw Quen, I can use Quen on my Obsidian and give it the skills, give it the voice

themes.title: pay per outcome
themes.claim: When each agent task has measurable ROI (you only pay for outcome, not subscriptions), scale is just replication — hundreds of agents clearing 70 cents each beat one human clearing thousands.

moments.quote: If you can make, for example, one dollar back with the cost of 30 cents
Because you can have hundreds of agents doing those, then you have the critical mass to be able to make tons of money.
activity makes sense, you can scale up and then you can make tons of money even the transaction is very small

themes.title: crypto needs a rebrand
themes.claim: Outside the bubble the word 'crypto' ends the conversation — builders now hide the crypto entirely or call for a rebrand before normal users will touch it.

moments.quote: You hear about it here and there. Once I stepped outside of the bubble, it hit me like a wall.
Now the brand is a bad brand. People associate it with scams, with gambling, with all these kind of things that are not good.
I'm specifically leaving out as much of the crypto bullshit
the problem is that the people who would like it otherwise I think are so turned off

themes.title: the incumbents eat it
themes.claim: AI-era categories are asymmetric bets that favor incumbents — startups burn runway on demand that isn't there while Stripe, Amazon, and the labs absorb whatever works.

moments.quote: Asymmetric bet in a positive way for an incumbents, and the reverse asymmetric bet for startups in a negative way for startups.
And by the time you get it and you get some customers, the incumbent is going to come eat your lunch and make the same thing.
The tension of software is so easy to make, but the big guys will fucking eat your lunch if you make something good enough.
